Steroids are often considered if kidney function does not recover after stopping the drug, but removing the trigger is the essential first step.
cards.q: A patient develops AKI with fever, rash and eosinophilia a week after starting penicillin. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: Glomerulonephritis, inflammation of the glomeruli. Red cell casts form inside the kidney, so they prove the blood is coming from the glomerulus, not the bladder. Get urgent nephrology input and a kidney biopsy, because treatment depends on the exact type and delay can mean irreversible scarring.
cards.q: A patient with AKI has red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells in the urine. What does this point to, and what is the next step?

cards.a: Pass a urinary catheter. This is post-renal AKI from obstruction, and relieving the blockage is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Do not give more fluids or diuretics first: the bladder is already full, and drainage often leads to rapid recovery of kidney function.
cards.q: An elderly man with AKI has a hugely distended bladder and has not passed urine for a day. What is the first step?

cards.a: Hepatorenal syndrome, where severe liver disease causes intense kidney vasoconstriction even though the kidneys themselves are structurally normal. Treat with albumin plus a vasoconstrictor such as terlipressin or noradrenaline to improve kidney blood flow. The definitive treatment is liver transplant, because the kidney failure is driven by the liver.
cards.q: A patient with advanced cirrhosis and ascites develops AKI with very low urine sodium and no improvement after albumin and stopping diuretics. What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Start dialysis. The classic indications are remembered as AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolyte problems (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload (fluid), and Uraemia (encephalopathy or pericarditis). When medical treatment fails, dialysis is the only way to remove potassium, acid and fluid.
cards.q: A patient with AKI is fluid overloaded, acidotic and has potassium of 7.0 that does not respond to medical treatment. What is the next step?

cards.a: Fluids were given without checking volume status. In AKI, the kidneys cannot excrete fluid, so extra fluid backs up into the lungs. Always assess volume first: dry mucous membranes and low blood pressure favour fluids, while crackles, raised jugular venous pressure and oedema mean the patient is already overloaded and needs diuretics or dialysis instead.
cards.q: A patient with AKI and pulmonary oedema is given more intravenous fluids and gets worse. What went wrong?

cards.a: Stop or reduce nephrotoxic drugs such as NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and contrast agents, and renally dose-adjust drugs cleared by the kidney, such as metformin and many antibiotics. In AKI the kidney clears drugs slowly, so normal doses accumulate and cause toxicity. Also hold ACE inhibitors and diuretics temporarily if blood pressure is low.
cards.q: A patient with AKI is on several medicines. What medication review should you do?

cards.a: Pre-renal AKI. When blood flow to the kidney falls, the kidney reabsorbs more urea along with sodium and water, so urea rises more than creatinine. In ATN the tubules are damaged and cannot reabsorb urea, so the ratio is usually below 20 to 1. The ratio supports, but does not prove, a pre-renal cause.
cards.q: A patient with AKI has a BUN to creatinine ratio above 20 to 1. What does this suggest?

cards.a: Arrange nephrology follow-up and recheck creatinine and electrolytes after discharge, and counsel them to avoid NSAIDs, dehydration and contrast where possible. Even after apparent recovery, AKI increases the long-term risk of chronic kidney disease, so the kidneys need monitoring rather than being forgotten.
cards.q: A patient is recovering from AKI and their creatinine is falling. What follow-up is needed?

cards.a: An ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB). These drugs lower pressure inside the glomerulus, which reduces protein loss and slows progression to kidney failure, beyond their effect on blood pressure alone. Check potassium and creatinine a week after starting.
cards.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) has 2 g of protein in the urine per day and rising blood pressure. What drug should you start, and why?

cards.a: Anaemia of CKD, because failing kidneys make too little erythropoietin, and iron deficiency is common. Replace iron first, then give an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent such as erythropoietin once iron stores are adequate. Aim for haemoglobin of 10 to 11.5 g/dL; pushing it higher increases the risk of clots and stroke.
cards.q: A patient with CKD stage 4 has haemoglobin of 9 g/dL, low iron and fatigue. What is the cause and the treatment?

cards.a: CKD mineral and bone disorder. Failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate or activate vitamin D, so phosphate rises, calcium falls and PTH rises, weakening bone. Treat with dietary phosphate restriction, phosphate binders with meals, and active vitamin D. Controlling phosphate early slows bone disease.
cards.q: A patient with CKD has high phosphate, low calcium and a very high parathyroid hormone (PTH). What is this, and how is it managed?

cards.a: Give oral sodium bicarbonate. The kidneys cannot excrete acid in CKD, so metabolic acidosis develops and worsens bone loss and muscle wasting. Correcting bicarbonate to above 22 slows CKD progression and improves symptoms. Watch for fluid retention, since bicarbonate is a sodium load.
cards.q: A patient with CKD has bicarbonate of 18 and feels unwell. What should you do?

cards.a: Start with dietary potassium restriction and review other drugs that raise potassium, such as spironolactone and trimethoprim. If potassium stays high, add a potassium binder such as patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, which removes potassium through the gut. Stop the ACE inhibitor only if potassium stays above 5.5 despite these measures or there are ECG changes.
cards.q: A patient with CKD has chronic potassium of 5.8 on an ACE inhibitor. How do you manage this without stopping a kidney-protective drug?

cards.a: Stop metformin when GFR falls below 30, because it accumulates and risks lactic acidosis, and stop the NSAID because it reduces kidney blood flow and raises potassium. In CKD, drugs cleared by the kidney need dose adjustment and nephrotoxins should be avoided, because the kidney has little reserve left.
cards.q: A patient with CKD stage 4 is still taking metformin and ibuprofen regularly. What should you change?

cards.a: Influenza every year, pneumococcal vaccine, and hepatitis B vaccine. CKD weakens the immune system and increases infection risk, and hepatitis B is especially important because dialysis exposes patients to blood. Vaccinate early, because the immune response is weaker once kidney failure is advanced.
cards.q: A patient with CKD asks which vaccinations they need. What should you recommend?

cards.a: Aim for blood pressure below 130/80, using an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first line. Tight blood pressure control plus reduced pressure inside the glomerulus slows kidney damage more than either alone. Check potassium and creatinine after starting and after each dose increase.
cards.q: A patient with CKD and diabetes has blood pressure 150/95 and proteinuria. What is the blood pressure target and the drug of choice?

cards.a: Refer for transplant assessment and start planning vascular access, such as an arteriovenous fistula, which takes months to mature. Early planning avoids starting dialysis through a temporary central line, which carries a high infection risk. Also discuss dialysis options and advance care planning with the patient.
cards.q: A patient with CKD stage 4 and GFR 20 is likely to need dialysis within a year. What should you arrange now?

cards.a: No, continue the statin. Patients with CKD have very high cardiovascular risk, and statins reduce heart attacks and strokes in CKD. Statins are not nephrotoxic, and stopping them removes protection from the commonest cause of death in CKD, which is cardiovascular disease, not kidney failure itself.
cards.q: A patient with CKD is on a statin. Their kidney function is worsening. Should you stop the statin?

cards.a: An SGLT2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. These drugs reduce pressure inside the glomerulus and slow the decline in kidney function in diabetic and non-diabetic CKD, on top of ACE inhibitors. They also reduce heart failure admissions. Check kidney function after starting, as a small initial dip in GFR is expected.
cards.q: A patient with diabetic kidney disease has proteinuria despite an ACE inhibitor. What drug should you add to slow progression?

cards.a: Give intravenous isotonic saline before and after the scan, use the lowest contrast dose possible, and hold NSAIDs and diuretics around the procedure. Hydration keeps the kidneys perfused and dilutes the contrast. Also hold metformin on the day of the scan and for 48 hours after, restarting only once kidney function is confirmed stable.
cards.q: A patient with CKD needs a contrast CT scan. How do you reduce the risk of contrast nephropathy?

cards.a: Uraemic pericarditis, inflammation of the pericardium from retained toxins. Dialysis is the treatment, because it removes the uraemic toxins causing the inflammation. Avoid pericardiocentesis unless there is tamponade, because the needle risks bleeding in a uraemic patient with platelet dysfunction.
cards.q: A patient with end-stage kidney disease develops chest pain, a pericardial friction rub and a large pericardial effusion. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome, caused by removing urea too quickly so water shifts into the brain. Prevent it by running the first dialysis sessions slowly with lower blood flow and a shorter duration, and by using a smaller dialyser. Headache, nausea and confusion during the first session should prompt slowing the treatment.
cards.q: A patient develops headache, nausea and confusion during their very first dialysis session. What is this and how is it prevented?

cards.a: Intradialytic hypotension, the commonest complication of haemodialysis. It happens when fluid is removed faster than it can move from the tissues into the blood. Slow the ultrafiltration rate, give a small fluid bolus, and reassess the target dry weight, which may be set too low.
cards.q: A patient's blood pressure repeatedly drops during haemodialysis. What is the most likely cause and the first step?

cards.a: Emergency dialysis. Potassium of 7 with peaked T waves is life-threatening and medical treatment may not work fast enough, especially in someone who has missed dialysis. Give calcium gluconate and insulin with glucose to protect the heart and shift potassium while dialysis is arranged, and do a continuous ECG.
cards.q: A patient on dialysis misses two sessions and arrives with potassium of 7.0 and peaked T waves. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Peritonitis, the commonest complication of peritoneal dialysis. Send the cloudy effluent for cell count, Gram stain and culture, then start intraperitoneal antibiotics immediately without waiting for the culture result. Delay risks loss of the peritoneal membrane and the patient having to switch to haemodialysis.
cards.q: A patient on peritoneal dialysis has cloudy dialysis fluid and abdominal pain. What is the diagnosis and the next step?

cards.a: An arteriovenous fistula. A fistula uses the patient's own vessels, lasts years and has a much lower infection risk than a central venous catheter. Plan it months before dialysis starts so it can mature. Catheters are for emergencies only, because they cause bloodstream infections and central vein narrowing.
cards.q: A patient is starting long-term haemodialysis. What vascular access should be planned, and why?

cards.a: Dialysis can remove lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol and salicylate, because these are small molecules not bound to protein. Haemodialysis is used when poisoning is severe, when the patient is acidotic or has a very high level, or when they cannot clear the drug themselves because of kidney failure.
cards.q: Which poisonings can be treated with haemodialysis?

cards.a: Give intravenous calcium gluconate first. It stabilises the heart membrane and prevents fatal arrhythmia within minutes, but it does not lower potassium at all. After calcium, use insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells, and arrange removal with dialysis or a potassium binder.
cards.q: A patient has potassium of 6.8 with peaked T waves and a widening QRS on ECG. What is the first drug to give, and what does it actually do?

cards.a: Insulin drives potassium into cells along with glucose. Give 10 units of regular insulin with glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia, and recheck potassium and glucose after an hour. This is a temporary shift, not removal, so potassium will rebound unless it is also removed by dialysis or a binder.
cards.q: Why do you give insulin and glucose together for hyperkalaemia, and what must you monitor afterwards?

cards.a: Potassium binders such as patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate remove potassium through the gut, but they take hours to work and are not for emergencies. They are for chronic or stable hyperkalaemia. In an emergency, calcium, insulin with glucose and dialysis are the treatments, because they act in minutes.
cards.q: A patient with potassium of 6.5 is stable with no ECG changes. Is a potassium binder such as patiromer suitable, and when would it not be enough?

cards.a: Sodium bicarbonate shifts potassium into cells and corrects the acidosis at the same time. It is most useful when hyperkalaemia comes with metabolic acidosis, such as in kidney failure. It is not a substitute for calcium when there are ECG changes, and it should not be given with calcium in the same line because they precipitate.
cards.q: A patient with kidney failure has potassium of 6.2 and a metabolic acidosis. Which treatment helps both problems?

cards.a: Pseudohyperkalaemia, a falsely high potassium from a haemolysed blood sample or from very high platelets or white cells breaking down in the tube. Repeat the sample and check the ECG: if the ECG is normal and the patient is well, the result is likely false. Do not give treatment for a laboratory artefact.
cards.q: A well patient has potassium of 6.4 but a completely normal ECG. What should you suspect, and what do you do next?

cards.a: Review the medicines: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, amiloride and trimethoprim all raise potassium by reducing its excretion. Stopping or reducing the culprit drug is often enough. Check kidney function too, because hyperkalaemia is much more likely when kidney function is impaired.
cards.q: A patient develops hyperkalaemia after starting new medicines. Which drugs are the usual culprits?

cards.a: Vomiting or diuretics, which cause loss of potassium and hydrogen ions, producing hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis. Replace potassium, correct the volume loss with saline, and stop the diuretic if possible. Check magnesium too, because low magnesium makes potassium hard to replace.
cards.q: A patient on a thiazide diuretic has potassium of 2.9 and a metabolic alkalosis. What is the cause and the treatment?

cards.a: Low potassium increases digoxin binding to heart muscle, so even a normal digoxin level can become toxic. Correct the potassium urgently, stop digoxin, and monitor the heart rhythm. This is why potassium must be kept normal in every patient taking digoxin.
cards.q: A patient on digoxin with potassium of 2.8 develops a new arrhythmia. Why is this dangerous, and what do you do?

cards.a: Magnesium is needed to retain potassium, so hypokalaemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced. Give magnesium first, then continue potassium replacement. This combination is common in alcohol use, diuretic use and diarrhoea, so always check magnesium when potassium is stubbornly low.
cards.q: A patient's potassium stays low despite large amounts of potassium replacement. What should you check?

cards.a: Primary aldosteronism, where excess aldosterone makes the kidney excrete potassium and retain sodium. Check plasma aldosterone and renin: aldosterone will be high and renin suppressed. Treat with spironolactone or surgery if an adenoma is found. This is a curable cause of hypertension, so do not miss it.
cards.q: A hypertensive patient has low potassium that keeps coming back. What diagnosis should you consider, and how do you test for it?

cards.a: Oral replacement for mild deficiency in a stable patient, and intravenous replacement with cardiac monitoring for severe deficiency or arrhythmia. Do not give intravenous potassium faster than 10 to 20 mEq per hour through a peripheral line, because rapid infusion can itself cause fatal arrhythmia. Recheck levels regularly.
cards.q: A patient has potassium of 2.6. When do you give oral versus intravenous potassium, and what is the safety limit?

cards.a: Give 3% hypertonic saline, ideally in intensive care. Seizures mean the brain is swelling from severe hyponatraemia, and this is the one situation where sodium must be corrected quickly, by about 4 to 6 mEq/L over a few hours. Then slow down to the usual limit of 8 to 10 per day to avoid osmotic demyelination.
cards.q: A patient has a seizure and sodium of 110. What is the immediate treatment?

cards.a: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). The body retains water inappropriately, diluting the sodium. Treat with fluid restriction first, and look for the cause: drugs, lung disease, malignancy and brain disease are common. Do not give saline, because the extra water will be retained and sodium will fall further.
cards.q: A patient with small cell lung cancer has sodium of 124, is clinically euvolaemic, with concentrated urine and high urine sodium. What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?

cards.a: Give isotonic saline. The patient has lost both salt and water, and the kidney is retaining what little sodium it has. Saline restores volume, which switches off ADH release and lets the kidney excrete the excess water. Fluid restriction would be wrong here, because the patient is already volume depleted.
cards.q: A patient with sodium of 126 is dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and low blood pressure after days of vomiting. What fluid should you give?

cards.a: Fluid restriction and treatment of the underlying heart failure or cirrhosis, such as diuretics. The body has too much total water, even though sodium is low, so giving saline would worsen the fluid overload. The low sodium reflects excess water diluting the blood, not a lack of salt.
cards.q: A patient with heart failure has sodium of 128 and swollen legs. Why is saline the wrong treatment?

cards.a: Stop the thiazide. Thiazides impair the kidney's ability to excrete free water, so sodium falls, especially in elderly patients. Sodium usually recovers within days of stopping the drug. Switch to a different antihypertensive, and avoid restarting thiazides in this patient.
cards.q: An elderly woman on bendroflumethiazide develops sodium of 122 and confusion. What is the most likely cause and the next step?

cards.a: Osmotic demyelination syndrome, where rapid correction strips myelin from brainstem fibres, causing weakness, difficulty speaking and swallowing, and sometimes locked-in syndrome. It is prevented by correcting sodium no faster than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours, and even slower in patients with alcohol use, malnutrition or liver disease.
cards.q: A patient's sodium is corrected from 110 to 128 in one day, and a few days later they develop slurred speech and weakness. What has happened, and how could it have been prevented?

cards.a: Pseudohyponatraemia, where very high lipids or proteins displace water in the blood sample, so sodium looks low even though the concentration in plasma water is normal. The serum osmolality is normal, which is the clue. Treat the underlying cause, not the sodium number.
cards.q: A patient with severe hyperlipidaemia has sodium of 126 but a normal serum osmolality. What is this, and what do you do?

cards.a: Calculate the free water deficit and replace it slowly with hypotonic fluid such as 5% dextrose or half-normal saline, aiming to lower sodium by no more than 10 to 12 mEq/L per day. The patient is water depleted, usually from not drinking enough or from diabetes insipidus. Correcting too fast can cause brain swelling.
cards.q: A patient has sodium of 160 after days of poor fluid intake. How do you correct it, and how fast?

cards.a: Central diabetes insipidus is a lack of ADH, while nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is resistance to ADH. Give desmopressin: in central DI the urine concentrates and output falls, but in nephrogenic DI nothing changes, because the kidney cannot respond. Central DI is treated with desmopressin, nephrogenic DI with thiazides and a low-salt diet.
cards.q: A patient passes huge volumes of dilute urine with high sodium. How do you tell central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?

cards.a: Do not correct sodium faster than 10 to 12 mEq/L per day. The brain has adapted to the high sodium by making osmoles, and rapid correction lets water rush in, causing cerebral oedema and seizures. Slow correction gives the brain time to shed those osmoles safely.
cards.q: Why must hypernatraemia be corrected slowly, and what is the safe rate?

cards.a: Give large volumes of intravenous normal saline first, which dilutes the calcium and increases its excretion in the urine. Once volume is restored, add a bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid to stop bone breakdown. Do not give a loop diuretic before fluids, because it will worsen dehydration and kidney function.
cards.q: A patient with calcium of 14 mg/dL is confused and dehydrated. What is the first treatment?

cards.a: Check PTH. If PTH is high, the cause is primary hyperparathyroidism. If PTH is low or suppressed, think of malignancy, where tumours release PTH-related protein, or vitamin D excess. This one test divides the two commonest causes and decides the workup.
cards.q: A patient has hypercalcaemia. Which single test best separates the two commonest causes?

cards.a: Give intravenous calcium gluconate. Tetany, perioral tingling and a positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign mean severe hypocalcaemia that can cause seizures and arrhythmia. Intravenous calcium stabilises the heart and nerves immediately. Then find the cause, such as low PTH, vitamin D deficiency or kidney failure, and replace calcium orally.
cards.q: A patient has tingling around the mouth, muscle cramps and a positive Chvostek sign with calcium of 6.5 mg/dL. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Hypoparathyroidism from damage to the parathyroid glands during surgery. Check PTH, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, and give calcium plus calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D, because without PTH the kidney cannot activate vitamin D. Most cases are temporary, but some are permanent.
cards.q: A patient develops low calcium two days after thyroid surgery. What is the likely cause and treatment?

cards.a: Shortened QT interval and risk of arrhythmia, and in severe cases heart block or cardiac arrest. Hypercalcaemia also causes confusion, constipation, kidney stones and bone pain. Always do an ECG in hypercalcaemia, and treat the calcium, not just the symptoms.
cards.q: What ECG changes does hypercalcaemia cause, and why does it matter?

cards.a: Stop the vitamin D and give intravenous fluids to dilute and excrete the calcium. Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone also help by reducing calcium absorption from the gut. This is important because vitamin D is fat-soluble, so levels stay high for weeks after stopping.
cards.q: A patient taking very high doses of vitamin D supplements develops hypercalcaemia. What should you do?

cards.a: Hypomagnesaemia, commonly from proton pump inhibitors, alcohol use, diuretics and diarrhoea. Replace magnesium intravenously if severe or symptomatic, because low magnesium causes arrhythmias, seizures and resistance to potassium replacement. Stop the offending drug where possible.
cards.q: A patient on long-term omeprazole has magnesium of 1.0 mg/dL, muscle cramps and an arrhythmia. What is the cause and treatment?

cards.a: Give intravenous calcium gluconate, which antagonises the effects of magnesium on the heart and nerves. Hypermagnesaemia usually happens in kidney failure when patients take magnesium-containing antacids or laxatives. Stop all magnesium sources, and use dialysis if kidney failure is severe.
cards.q: A patient with kidney failure who took magnesium-containing laxatives has magnesium of 5 mg/dL, low blood pressure and a slow heart rate. What is the antidote?

cards.a: Refeeding syndrome. When a starved patient starts eating again, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, so blood levels crash. Replace phosphate before and during refeeding, check electrolytes daily, and start feeding slowly. Low phosphate can cause respiratory failure because the diaphragm cannot make enough ATP.
cards.q: A malnourished patient develops low phosphate, low potassium and low magnesium two days after starting to eat again. What is this, and what do you do?

cards.a: Dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate binders taken with meals, such as calcium carbonate or sevelamer. Failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate, so it accumulates and drives up PTH, weakening bone. Binders trap phosphate in the gut so it is passed in the stool instead of being absorbed.
cards.q: A patient with CKD has phosphate of 7 mg/dL. How do you lower it?

cards.a: Phosphate is needed to make ATP, so severe deficiency weakens the diaphragm and makes it hard to wean from a ventilator. Replace phosphate intravenously in a critically ill patient, and recheck levels frequently. Also check potassium and magnesium, which often fall together.
cards.q: A patient in intensive care cannot be weaned from the ventilator and has phosphate of 1.2 mg/dL. How are these linked?

cards.a: MUDPILES: Methanol, Uraemia, Diabetic ketoacidosis, Paraldehyde, Iron or Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylate. When the anion gap is high, run through this list and look for the cause: check glucose and ketones, lactate, kidney function, drug history and the osmolal gap. Treating the underlying cause matters more than the number itself.
cards.q: A patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. What causes should you consider?

cards.a: Treat the cause: restore perfusion with fluids and treat the underlying sepsis or shock. Bicarbonate is not routinely given, because it does not improve outcomes and can worsen intracellular acidosis. The lactate falls once tissues are perfused again, so recheck it to follow the response.
cards.q: A patient in septic shock has lactate of 8 and a metabolic acidosis. Should you give bicarbonate?

cards.a: Give large volumes of intravenous fluids, start insulin, and replace potassium aggressively, because insulin drives potassium into cells. The anion gap should close as ketones clear. Do not give bicarbonate routinely, and do not stop insulin even when glucose normalises: switch to dextrose-containing fluids and continue insulin until the gap closes.
cards.q: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has glucose of 500, bicarbonate of 8 and potassium of 4.5. What are the priorities?

cards.a: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis comes from losing bicarbonate in diarrhoea or failing to excrete acid in renal tubular acidosis. Check the urine anion gap: a positive value means the kidney is not excreting ammonium, pointing to renal tubular acidosis, while a negative value points to diarrhoea. The treatment differs, so the distinction matters.
cards.q: A patient has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. How do you tell diarrhoea from renal tubular acidosis?

cards.a: Type 1, distal renal tubular acidosis. The distal tubule cannot excrete acid, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidosis, and potassium is lost in the urine. Patients develop kidney stones and bone disease from chronic acidosis. Treat with oral bicarbonate or citrate, and replace potassium.
cards.q: A patient has metabolic acidosis, low potassium, kidney stones and urine pH of 6.5. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is this?

cards.a: Type 2, proximal renal tubular acidosis. The proximal tubule fails to reabsorb bicarbonate, so it is lost in the urine, and there is often Fanconi syndrome with loss of phosphate, glucose and amino acids. Treat with large doses of bicarbonate and replace phosphate. The cause is often a drug or a genetic disorder.
cards.q: A patient has metabolic acidosis with glycosuria despite normal blood glucose, phosphaturia and low potassium. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is this?

cards.a: Type 4 renal tubular acidosis. Aldosterone deficiency or resistance means the kidney cannot excrete potassium or acid, so potassium rises and acidosis develops. It is common in diabetes and CKD. Treat by stopping drugs that raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors and spironolactone, and give bicarbonate or a loop diuretic.
cards.q: A diabetic patient with CKD has high potassium and a mild metabolic acidosis. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is this, and what causes it?

cards.a: Vomiting or nasogastric suction causes metabolic alkalosis because stomach acid is lost, and the urine chloride is low because the kidney is holding on to chloride. Diuretics also cause metabolic alkalosis, but the urine chloride is high because the drug forces chloride out. Urine chloride therefore separates the two commonest causes.
cards.q: A patient has metabolic alkalosis. How does urine chloride tell you whether the cause is vomiting or diuretics?

cards.a: Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation, usually an acute exacerbation of COPD. Treat the cause: bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if infected, and non-invasive ventilation such as BiPAP to blow off carbon dioxide. Do not give bicarbonate, because the problem is carbon dioxide retention, not bicarbonate loss.
cards.q: A patient with COPD has pH 7.28, PaCO2 70 and bicarbonate 30. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Common causes are anxiety, pain, sepsis, pulmonary embolism and early salicylate poisoning. Treat the underlying cause rather than the pH: reassure the anxious patient, treat the infection or embolism, and the breathing will settle. Do not give bicarbonate.
cards.q: A patient is breathing fast with pH 7.52 and PaCO2 25. What is the acid-base disorder, and what causes it?

cards.a: Use the delta ratio: change in anion gap divided by change in bicarbonate. A ratio near 1 means a pure high anion gap acidosis. A ratio below 1 means there is also a normal anion gap acidosis, and a ratio above 2 means there is also a metabolic alkalosis. It reveals a second disorder hiding behind the first.
cards.q: A patient has a high anion gap acidosis but the bicarbonate has not fallen as much as you expect. How do you check for a second acid-base disorder?

cards.a: Salicylate poisoning causes a mixed disorder: respiratory alkalosis from stimulation of the breathing centre, plus a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from salicylate itself. Give intravenous fluids and sodium bicarbonate to alkalinise the urine, which traps salicylate and increases its excretion. Haemodialysis is needed if levels are very high or the patient deteriorates.
cards.q: A patient who took an overdose of aspirin has tinnitus, rapid breathing, pH 7.45, low bicarbonate and a high anion gap. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning. These alcohols are metabolised to toxic acids, causing a high anion gap acidosis with a high osmolal gap. Give fomepizole to block the enzyme that creates the toxic metabolites, and arrange haemodialysis to remove the poison and correct the acidosis. Do not wait for confirmation if the history is strong.
cards.q: A patient has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, a high osmolal gap and visual disturbance after drinking moonshine. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. It appears 1 to 3 weeks after a streptococcal throat or skin infection, with haematuria, oedema, hypertension and low C3 that recovers over weeks. Treatment is supportive: control blood pressure and fluid overload. It is usually self-limited, so immunosuppression is not needed.
cards.q: A child develops blood in the urine, swollen face and high blood pressure two weeks after a sore throat. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: IgA nephropathy, the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide. Haematuria appears within days of a respiratory infection, because IgA deposits in the glomerulus. Most patients need only blood pressure control and an ACE inhibitor to reduce proteinuria; steroids are reserved for progressive disease.
cards.q: A young man has visible blood in his urine every time he gets a cold. What is the likely diagnosis?

cards.a: Membranous nephropathy, usually from antibodies against the PLA2R antigen on podocytes. It causes nephrotic syndrome in adults. Work up for secondary causes, especially malignancy, hepatitis B and lupus. Treatment is an ACE inhibitor plus immunosuppression if proteinuria is severe or kidney function is falling.
cards.q: An adult has nephrotic syndrome with a kidney biopsy showing thickened glomerular basement membrane and PLA2R antibodies. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Minimal change disease. It is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, the biopsy looks normal on light microscopy, and electron microscopy shows effaced podocyte foot processes. It responds dramatically to steroids, so most children remit quickly. Adults can get it too, often triggered by drugs or lymphoma.
cards.q: A 5-year-old develops sudden nephrotic syndrome and the kidney biopsy looks normal under the light microscope. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). It causes nephrotic syndrome but, unlike minimal change disease, it often resists steroids and progresses to kidney failure. Secondary causes include HIV, obesity and sickle cell disease. Treat the underlying cause, control blood pressure and proteinuria with an ACE inhibitor, and consider steroids only for primary disease.
cards.q: An adult with nephrotic syndrome has scarring in some glomeruli on biopsy and does not respond to steroids. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: Lupus nephritis. Kidney involvement in SLE is common and often silent, so screen every lupus patient with urine protein and sediment. The biopsy class determines treatment: mild disease needs an ACE inhibitor, while proliferative disease needs steroids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide. Do not treat without a biopsy, because the regimen depends on the class.
cards.q: A young woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops proteinuria and red cell casts. What is the next step?

cards.a: ANCA-associated vasculitis, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. The biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, meaning there is little immune staining. Treatment is urgent immunosuppression with steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Delay risks irreversible kidney failure and lung haemorrhage.
cards.q: A patient with sinusitis, coughing blood and rapidly rising creatinine has a kidney biopsy showing crescents with almost no immune deposits. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Anti-GBM disease, also called Goodpasture syndrome. Antibodies attack the basement membrane of kidney and lung, causing haematuria with haemoptysis. Treat urgently with plasmapheresis to remove the antibodies plus steroids and cyclophosphamide to stop new ones. Early treatment can save the kidneys; delay usually means dialysis.
cards.q: A patient has blood in the urine, coughs up blood, and the kidney biopsy shows linear IgG along the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Diabetic nephropathy, from years of high blood sugar damaging the glomerulus. Screen with urine albumin every year from diagnosis in type 2 diabetes and after 5 years in type 1. Treat with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, an SGLT2 inhibitor, tight glucose control and blood pressure below 130/80. Once proteinuria is heavy, it rarely reverses, so prevention matters.
cards.q: A diabetic patient has 500 mg of albumin in the urine per day and a rising creatinine. What is the diagnosis, and how do you slow it down?

cards.a: Nephrotic syndrome causes loss of clotting inhibitors such as antithrombin in the urine, while the liver makes more clotting factors, so blood clots easily. Renal vein thrombosis causes sudden flank pain, worsening proteinuria and a swollen kidney. Treat with anticoagulation, and suspect it whenever a nephrotic patient has new flank pain.
cards.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden severe flank pain and worsening kidney function. What complication should you suspect?

cards.a: Give anticoagulation when albumin is very low, especially below 2.0 to 2.5 g/dL, or when there is a previous clot, atrial fibrillation or another risk factor. The risk of clotting is high because antithrombin is lost in the urine. Prophylactic anticoagulation is not routine for all nephrotic patients, so balance the clot risk against bleeding risk.
cards.q: Which patients with nephrotic syndrome should receive anticoagulation?

cards.a: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, where kidney function falls over days to weeks with red cell casts and often crescents on biopsy. Get an urgent kidney biopsy and start immunosuppression quickly, because every day of delay means more scarring. Do not watch and wait: this is a kidney emergency.
cards.q: A patient's creatinine doubles in two weeks and the urine shows red cell casts. What is this, and what must you do urgently?

cards.a: Add a thiazide diuretic for sequential nephron blockade. The loop diuretic blocks sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle, but the distal tubule then reabsorbs the extra sodium. A thiazide blocks that distal reabsorption, so the combination works when a loop alone no longer does. Watch potassium and kidney function closely.
cards.q: A patient with heart failure is no longer responding to high-dose furosemide. What should you add, and why does it work?

cards.a: A loop diuretic such as furosemide. Thiazides lose their effect when GFR falls below 30, because they cannot reach their site of action in adequate amounts. Loop diuretics still work in advanced CKD, though higher doses may be needed. This is a common exam point: thiazides fail in severe CKD, loops do not.
cards.q: A patient with CKD and GFR 20 has fluid overload. Why is a thiazide the wrong choice, and what should you use instead?

cards.a: Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist. It reduces mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction by blocking aldosterone-driven fibrosis and sodium retention. Monitor potassium and creatinine, because spironolactone raises potassium, especially when combined with an ACE inhibitor.
cards.q: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is already on an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker. What drug should you add to reduce mortality?

cards.a: Acetazolamide blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so bicarbonate is lost in the urine and a metabolic acidosis develops. It is used for glaucoma and altitude sickness, and sometimes to treat metabolic alkalosis. Do not use it in severe kidney failure, because it cannot work there and acidosis worsens.
cards.q: A patient taking acetazolamide develops a metabolic acidosis. Why does this happen, and what is the drug used for?

cards.a: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that draws water into the kidney tubule and also reduces brain swelling. It is used for raised intracranial pressure. Give it cautiously in kidney failure, because it can itself cause AKI and pulmonary oedema if it accumulates, and monitor sodium and osmolality.
cards.q: A patient with a head injury and raised intracranial pressure is given mannitol. How does it work, and what is the risk in kidney failure?

cards.a: Give isotonic saline before and after the procedure, use the lowest contrast dose, and hold NSAIDs and diuretics. Hydration is the only measure proven to reduce contrast nephropathy. N-acetylcysteine and bicarbonate are not routinely recommended, so do not rely on them.
cards.q: A patient with CKD needs a contrast angiogram. What is the one proven way to prevent contrast nephropathy?

cards.a: Creatinine typically rises 24 to 72 hours after contrast and peaks at 3 to 5 days, then recovers over a week or two if the injury is mild. This timing helps distinguish contrast nephropathy from other causes of AKI. Recheck creatinine at 48 to 72 hours after the procedure in high-risk patients.
cards.q: When does creatinine peak after contrast exposure?

cards.a: Give aggressive intravenous isotonic fluids to maintain a high urine output, aiming for around 200 mL per hour initially, so myoglobin is flushed out before it blocks the tubules. Check potassium, calcium and phosphate frequently, because rhabdomyolysis causes dangerous electrolyte shifts. Watch for compartment syndrome in the affected limbs.
cards.q: A patient is found after lying on the floor for hours with dark urine, very high creatine kinase and rising creatinine. What is the treatment?

cards.a: Myoglobinuria. The urine dipstick detects the haem pigment in myoglobin, but microscopy shows no red cells, because the pigment comes from damaged muscle, not blood. This distinguishes rhabdomyolysis from bleeding in the urinary tract, and it means the kidneys are at risk from myoglobin blocking the tubules.
cards.q: A patient's urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. What does this mean?

cards.a: Dialysis is needed when hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload do not respond to medical treatment, or when there is severe uraemia. Most rhabdomyolysis is managed with fluids alone, so dialysis is not routine. The decision is based on complications, not on the creatine kinase number itself.
cards.q: When does a patient with rhabdomyolysis need dialysis?

cards.a: Give large volumes of intravenous fluids early, ideally before the patient is extricated if possible, because releasing the pressure lets potassium and myoglobin flood into the blood and can cause fatal arrhythmia and AKI. Monitor potassium and the ECG continuously during rescue.
cards.q: A patient is trapped under rubble with a crushed leg. Why should fluids be started before the limb is freed?

cards.a: Relieve the obstruction first, usually with a urinary catheter or a stent. Post-renal AKI is one of the few reversible causes of kidney failure, and the longer the obstruction lasts, the more likely the damage becomes permanent. Antibiotics alone will not help if urine cannot drain.
cards.q: A patient with AKI has a kidney stone blocking the ureter and a fever. What is the priority: antibiotics or relieving the obstruction?

cards.a: Bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis of a single functioning kidney. An ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, which is how the kidney maintains filtration when its blood supply is narrowed, so the drug can precipitate AKI. Suspect it when creatinine jumps after starting an ACE inhibitor, or when there is flash pulmonary oedema with resistant hypertension.
cards.q: A patient with resistant hypertension and flash pulmonary oedema develops AKI after starting an ACE inhibitor. What should you suspect?

cards.a: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. The kidneys enlarge with cysts, and patients develop hypertension, haematuria and kidney failure over decades. Screen for berry aneurysms with brain imaging if there is a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid haemorrhage. Tolvaptan can slow cyst growth in selected patients with rapid progression.
cards.q: A patient has massively enlarged kidneys full of cysts, hypertension and a father who died of a brain bleed. What is the diagnosis, and what screening is needed?

cards.a: Drink plenty of fluids, reduce salt, and use a thiazide diuretic, which lowers calcium in the urine. Calcium oxalate is the commonest stone type, and most stones form because urine is too concentrated or too rich in calcium. For uric acid stones, alkalinise the urine with potassium citrate, because uric acid dissolves better in alkaline urine.
cards.q: A patient keeps forming calcium oxalate kidney stones. How do you prevent them, and how does prevention differ for uric acid stones?
A kidney transplant patient develops rising creatinine two weeks after surgery. What drug level should you check first, and why?
cards.a: Check the tacrolimus level. Tacrolimus and ciclosporin are calcineurin inhibitors that constrict the kidney's blood vessels and are nephrotoxic, especially at high levels. If the level is high, reduce the dose and kidney function often recovers. A kidney biopsy is needed if the level is therapeutic, because rejection looks similar.

cards.q: A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops pneumonia. Why are these patients prone to serious infections, and what prevention is needed?
cards.a: Nephrotic syndrome causes loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors in the urine, so the immune system is weakened, especially against encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Give pneumococcal and influenza vaccines, and treat infections early and aggressively, because they can be severe and can also trigger a relapse of the nephrotic syndrome.

cards.q: A patient with SIADH has sodium of 122 that does not improve with fluid restriction. What is the next step?
cards.a: Add a vasopressin receptor antagonist such as tolvaptan, or oral urea, which increase free water excretion. Fluid restriction is first line, but when it fails or cannot be tolerated, blocking ADH lets the kidney excrete water and raise sodium. Correct slowly, no more than 8 to 10 mEq/L per day, to avoid osmotic demyelination.

Glucose over 250 mg/dL, pH below 7.30, bicarbonate below 18, and ketones in blood or urine. It is caused by insulin deficiency, often triggered by infection or missed insulin. Treatment: IV fluids first, then fixed-rate insulin, and replace potassium — check potassium before starting insulin, because insulin lowers it further.
cards.q: What are the diagnostic criteria for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

cards.a: DKA: glucose usually 250-600, pH low, ketones present, patient often young with type 1 diabetes. HHS: glucose very high, often over 600, pH near normal, ketones absent or minimal, severe dehydration, patient often older with type 2 diabetes. Both need IV fluids; DKA needs insulin sooner.
cards.q: How do you tell DKA from hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)?

cards.a: Diabetes is diagnosed if any one is true: HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour glucose 200 mg/dL or more after a glucose load, or random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms. HbA1c shows average glucose over 2-3 months.
cards.q: What are the diagnostic cut-offs for diabetes?

cards.a: Low cortisol with high ACTH means primary adrenal failure (Addison's disease) — the adrenal gland itself has failed. Low cortisol with low ACTH means secondary — the pituitary is not sending ACTH. Addison's: fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, high potassium, low sodium, and darkening of the skin. Treatment is hydrocortisone, with extra dose in illness.
cards.q: How do you tell primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?

cards.a: Too much cortisol. Causes: long-term steroid use (most common), pituitary tumour (Cushing's disease), adrenal tumour, or ectopic ACTH from a lung cancer. Signs: central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple stretch marks, high blood pressure, high glucose, weak muscles, easy bruising.
cards.q: What causes Cushing syndrome, and what does it look like?

cards.a: High calcium (over 10.5 mg/dL) is usually from hyperparathyroidism or cancer. Symptoms: stones (kidney stones), bones (bone pain), groans (abdominal pain, constipation), moans (confusion, depression). Treatment: IV fluids first, then a bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronate). Calcitonin works fast but only for a short time.
cards.q: What causes high calcium, and how is it treated?

cards.a: SIADH: too much ADH, so the body holds water, sodium falls, urine is concentrated, patient is clinically euvolaemic (not dry, not overloaded). Diabetes insipidus: too little ADH (central) or kidneys do not respond to ADH (nephrogenic) — patient makes large amounts of very dilute urine and is very thirsty.
cards.q: How do you tell SIADH from diabetes insipidus?

cards.a: Thyroid storm is life-threatening overactive thyroid: high fever, fast heart rate, confusion, agitation. Treatment: 1. Beta-blocker (propranolol) to slow the heart, 2. Propylthiouracil (PTU) to block new thyroid hormone, 3. Steroids, 4. Iodine — given AFTER the PTU, at least 1 hour later, otherwise iodine feeds hormone production.
cards.q: What is the treatment for thyroid storm, and in what order?

cards.a: It is a tumour of the adrenal medulla that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts. Symptoms: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and very high blood pressure. Diagnose with plasma or urine metanephrines. Treatment: alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) FIRST, then beta-blocker — never beta-blocker alone, because that leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and blood pressure can rise further.
cards.q: What is phaeochromocytoma, and what is the key treatment rule?

cards.a: A serious skin reaction to drugs, with fever, eosinophilia (high eosinophils) and internal organ involvement (liver, kidney). It starts 2-6 weeks after starting a drug like allopurinol, carbamazepine or phenytoin. Stop the drug immediately, give steroids if severe. It is different from a simple drug rash — organs are involved.
cards.q: What is DRESS syndrome?

cards.a: Hypothyroidism: low T4, high TSH, weight gain, cold intolerance, slow heart rate, constipation, fatigue. Treat with levothyroxine. Hyperthyroidism: high T4, low TSH, weight loss, heat intolerance, fast heart rate, tremor, diarrhoea. Treat with methimazole, beta-blocker, and consider radioiodine or surgery.
cards.q: How do thyroid function tests differ in hypo- and hyperthyroidism?

cards.a: IV isotonic fluids (normal saline) first — usually 1 litre over the first hour. DKA patients are severely dehydrated, and fluids restore circulation and start lowering glucose. Insulin comes after fluids are running and potassium has been checked, because insulin without fluids and with low potassium is dangerous.
cards.q: A patient in DKA has a blood pressure of 90/60 and dry mucous membranes. What is the very first treatment, before insulin?

cards.a: Replace potassium first and delay insulin until potassium is above 3.3 mmol/L. Insulin drives potassium into cells, so starting it with a low potassium can cause a fatal arrhythmia. Recheck potassium frequently — DKA treatment shifts potassium fast.
cards.q: A patient in DKA has a potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. What must you do before starting the insulin infusion?

cards.a: Keep the insulin infusion running and add dextrose to the IV fluids (switch to dextrose-containing fluids). Stopping insulin while ketones remain lets ketoacidosis continue — the insulin is there to clear ketones, not just to lower glucose, so you add sugar to allow insulin to continue safely.
cards.q: During DKA treatment the glucose has fallen to 240 mg/dL but ketones are still present. What should you do with the insulin and fluids?

cards.a: When the anion gap has closed, bicarbonate is above 15, pH is above 7.30, and ketones have cleared, with the patient eating. Do not stop on glucose alone — glucose normalises long before ketones clear, and stopping early causes relapse.
cards.q: How do you know DKA has resolved and it is safe to stop the IV insulin infusion?

cards.a: No — bicarbonate is not routine in DKA, even with a low pH. Fluids and insulin correct the acidosis. Bicarbonate is only considered when pH is below 6.9, because it can worsen low potassium, cause fluid overload, and paradoxically worsen acidosis inside cells.
cards.q: Should you give IV bicarbonate routinely in DKA?

cards.a: Suspect cerebral oedema — the most feared complication of DKA in children. Get urgent help, give mannitol or hypertonic saline, reduce the fluid rate, and get an urgent CT head after stabilisation. Drowsiness or headache during DKA treatment is a red flag, not just dehydration.
cards.q: A child with new type 1 diabetes in DKA becomes drowsy with a headache during treatment. What complication should you suspect and what do you do?

cards.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS). Give IV isotonic fluids first — these patients have a huge fluid deficit. Insulin is started later and more cautiously than in DKA, only after fluids are running, because rapid glucose falls can cause brain swelling.
cards.q: A 78-year-old with type 2 diabetes arrives confused, severely dehydrated, glucose 950 mg/dL, pH 7.35, no ketones. What is the diagnosis and the first treatment?

cards.a: Slowly — aim for a glucose fall of about 50 to 70 mg/dL per hour and a gradual fall in osmolality. Rapid correction can cause cerebral oedema. Fluids alone usually bring glucose down substantially before insulin is even needed.
cards.q: In HHS, how fast should you lower the blood glucose and osmolality?

cards.a: Euglycaemic DKA — ketoacidosis caused by the SGLT2 inhibitor despite a near-normal glucose. Do not rule out DKA just because glucose is not high. Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor, give fluids, insulin and dextrose together, and check ketones.
cards.q: A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) has nausea, abdominal pain and a pH of 7.25, but glucose is only 180 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis?

cards.a: DKA is almost always triggered by something — infection, missed insulin, heart attack, stroke or surgery. Treating only the acidosis while missing a pneumonia or MI leaves the trigger driving relapse. Check infection screen, ECG, and ask about missed insulin doses in every case.
cards.q: A patient in DKA is also found to have a fever and a urinary infection. Why must you search for a precipitant in every DKA admission?

cards.a: Give the first subcutaneous insulin dose 1 to 2 hours before stopping the IV infusion (long-acting insulin can be given earlier, even on admission). Without overlap there is a gap with no insulin, and ketosis can return within hours.
cards.q: A patient with DKA is now eating and the anion gap is closed. How do you switch from IV insulin to subcutaneous insulin?

cards.a: Because total body potassium is low in DKA even when the blood level looks normal — acidosis pushes potassium out of cells. Fluids and insulin then drive it back in, so potassium can crash suddenly. Frequent checks prevent a dangerous fall.
cards.q: In DKA, why do you check potassium every 2 to 4 hours even when the first level looks normal?

cards.a: Very high glucose pulls water out of cells and dilutes sodium, so the measured sodium underestimates the true sodium. Correct it for glucose (add about 1.6 mmol/L for every 100 mg/dL glucose above normal). What matters is the osmolality and the fluid deficit — replace fluid slowly and monitor sodium as glucose falls.
cards.q: A patient with HHS has a sodium of 155 mmol/L. Why is the measured sodium misleading, and what matters more?

cards.a: Yes — replace phosphate when it is low, especially if the patient is weak or has breathing difficulty. Insulin drives phosphate into cells just like potassium, and severe hypophosphataemia causes muscle weakness, respiratory failure and haemolysis.
cards.q: A patient in DKA has a phosphate of 1.5 mg/dL on day 2 of treatment. Should you replace it, and why?

cards.a: Metformin — it is first-line for type 2 diabetes. It lowers glucose without causing hypoglycaemia or weight gain, and it is cheap and well studied. Start it alongside diet and exercise, unless the patient has a contraindication.
cards.q: A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic with an HbA1c of 7.8% and no heart or kidney disease needs a first drug. Which drug and why?

cards.a: Hold metformin when there is acute kidney injury, severe illness, dehydration, or around contrast if kidney function is poor. Metformin is cleared by the kidneys, and if the kidneys fail it accumulates and can cause lactic acidosis. Restart once the patient is eating and kidney function is back to baseline.
cards.q: When must you hold metformin around a CT scan with contrast or acute illness?

cards.a: No — stop metformin when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min, because the risk of lactic acidosis rises sharply. Between 30 and 45, use a reduced dose and monitor kidney function closely. At this level, other drugs such as insulin or a GLP-1 agonist are safer.
cards.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes has an eGFR of 25 mL/min. Can they stay on metformin?

cards.a: Vitamin B12 deficiency — metformin reduces B12 absorption. Check a B12 level before blaming diabetic neuropathy, because B12 deficiency is reversible with replacement while neuropathy is not.
cards.q: A patient on metformin for 5 years develops numbness and tingling in the feet. What drug-related cause should you check?

cards.a: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor (such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin). It lowers heart failure admissions and death and protects the kidneys, on top of lowering glucose. This benefit is independent of glucose control — it is now a heart failure drug, not just a diabetes drug.
cards.q: A type 2 diabetic with heart failure and an HbA1c of 8.0% is on metformin alone. Which drug should you add and why?

cards.a: Stop it 3 days before surgery (4 days for ertugliflozin). Surgery and fasting raise the risk of euglycaemic DKA, which is hard to spot because glucose stays near normal. Restart once the patient is eating normally after surgery.
cards.q: A patient is due for elective surgery in 3 days and takes dapagliflozin. What should you do with the SGLT2 inhibitor and why?

cards.a: A GLP-1 receptor agonist (such as semaglutide). It lowers glucose, causes significant weight loss and reduces cardiovascular events. Warn about nausea, vomiting and early fullness, and that it slows stomach emptying — tell the anaesthetist before any procedure, as aspiration risk is higher.
cards.q: A type 2 diabetic with obesity and an HbA1c of 8.5% wants a drug that helps weight loss. Which class fits best, and what must you warn about?

cards.a: Patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2, those with gastroparesis, and those with a history of pancreatitis. GLP-1 drugs are contraindicated in medullary thyroid cancer because of a tumour signal in animal studies, and they worsen slow stomach emptying.
cards.q: Which patients should NOT get a GLP-1 receptor agonist?

cards.a: Yes — add a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit, even though the HbA1c is close to target. In patients with heart disease these drugs reduce heart attacks, strokes and death beyond glucose lowering, so the indication is the heart disease, not the HbA1c.
cards.q: A type 2 diabetic has established atherosclerotic heart disease and an HbA1c of 7.4% on metformin. Should you intensify treatment, and with what?

cards.a: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor. It slows kidney disease progression and reduces albuminuria on top of the ACE inhibitor. This combination is now standard kidney protection in diabetic kidney disease.
cards.q: A type 2 diabetic with albumin in the urine and an eGFR of 45 is on metformin and an ACE inhibitor. What should you add to protect the kidneys?

cards.a: Sulfonylureas force the pancreas to release insulin regardless of glucose level, so they cause hypoglycaemia — especially in older patients, those with kidney disease, or those who skip meals. Switch to a drug that does not cause hypoglycaemia, such as metformin, a DPP-4 inhibitor, GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor.
cards.q: A patient on a sulfonylurea (glipizide) keeps having low blood sugars. What is the mechanism and what should you change?

cards.a: Admit and give a continuous dextrose infusion plus octreotide. Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia can last 12 to 24 hours because the drug keeps stimulating insulin release; octreotide suppresses insulin secretion. A single dextrose bolus wears off and the sugar crashes again.
cards.q: A patient took an overdose of glibenclamide and has recurrent hypoglycaemia despite dextrose boluses. What is the definitive treatment?

cards.a: Pioglitazone (a thiazolidinedione) causes fluid retention and weight gain and worsens heart failure — it is contraindicated in heart failure. It also increases fracture risk. Choose an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist instead.
cards.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure is offered pioglitazone. Why should you avoid it?

cards.a: Weight gain: insulin, sulfonylureas and thiazolidinediones. Weight loss: GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors. Weight neutral: metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors. This matters when choosing drugs for a patient with obesity.
cards.q: Which diabetes drugs cause weight gain and which cause weight loss?

cards.a: Stop the DPP-4 inhibitor. It can cause severe joint pain and has been linked to pancreatitis. These drugs are weight-neutral and low risk for hypoglycaemia, but pancreatitis or severe arthralgia means stopping and choosing another class.
cards.q: A patient on a DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin) develops severe joint pain and a history of pancreatitis is noted. What should you do?

cards.a: Start insulin. When HbA1c is very high (above 10%) with symptoms of high glucose, oral drugs act too slowly and the patient is catabolic. Insulin brings glucose down fast and rests the pancreas; oral drugs can be added or substituted later once controlled.
cards.q: A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic has an HbA1c of 11% with weight loss, thirst and frequent urination. What is the initial treatment?

cards.a: A basal-bolus regimen — long-acting basal insulin plus mealtime rapid-acting insulin, with a correction scale. Sliding scale alone chases high sugars after they happen instead of preventing them, and it leads to worse control and longer stays.
cards.q: A hospitalised patient with type 2 diabetes is on sliding-scale insulin only and sugars stay high. What regimen should replace it?

cards.a: Never stop insulin completely in type 1 diabetes — they will go into DKA. Continue basal insulin (often at a reduced dose) with an IV insulin infusion or a variable-rate infusion while fasting, and monitor glucose and ketones hourly.
cards.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes is admitted for surgery and will be nil by mouth. How do you manage their insulin?

cards.a: Insulin is the drug of choice in pregnancy — it does not cross the placenta. Stop SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists and sulfonylureas, and review metformin with the obstetrician (it is sometimes continued). Tight glucose control in pregnancy prevents birth defects and macrosomia.
cards.q: A pregnant patient with type 2 diabetes asks which diabetes drugs are safe in pregnancy. What do you advise?

cards.a: Steroids raise glucose mainly in the afternoon and evening, so use insulin that matches that pattern — often intermediate-acting (NPH) insulin in the morning. Monitor sugars, and expect glucose to normalise when steroids are tapered. Do not rely on metformin alone for severe steroid hyperglycaemia.
cards.q: A patient on high-dose prednisolone develops blood sugars of 300 mg/dL. How do you manage steroid-induced hyperglycaemia?

cards.a: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (such as glucose tablets or juice), recheck in 15 minutes, and repeat until glucose is above 70 mg/dL — the 15-15 rule. Once recovered, give a snack with protein if the next meal is more than an hour away. Do not give chocolate or biscuits as first treatment — the fat slows absorption.
cards.q: A conscious patient with diabetes has a glucose of 55 mg/dL and is sweaty and shaky. What is the immediate treatment?

cards.a: Give IV dextrose (25 g as D50) if IV access is available; if not, give intramuscular glucagon. Never put food or drink in the mouth of an unconscious patient — they will aspirate. Once awake, give oral carbohydrate and find the cause.
cards.q: A diabetic patient is unconscious with a glucose of 40 mg/dL. What is the treatment, and what must you never do?

cards.a: Hypoglycaemia unawareness — repeated lows blunt the warning symptoms, so the first sign may be confusion or collapse. Relax the glucose targets temporarily, review the insulin regimen, and avoid lows for several weeks, which can restore awareness.
cards.q: A patient with type 1 diabetes no longer feels warning symptoms before severe low blood sugar. What is this called and how do you manage it?

cards.a: Reduce the evening basal (long-acting) insulin dose and review bedtime glucose. Nocturnal hypoglycaemia is often caused by too much basal insulin or a missed evening snack after exercise. A continuous glucose monitor can catch lows that happen overnight.
cards.q: A patient on basal insulin wakes sweaty with morning headaches and low fasting sugars. What is the likely problem and what should you change?

cards.a: Whipple's triad: symptoms of low glucose, a documented low glucose at the time, and relief with glucose. Confirm with a supervised 72-hour fast showing high insulin and C-peptide with low glucose, then localise with imaging. Treatment is surgical removal of the insulinoma.
cards.q: A patient has recurrent fasting hypoglycaemia with confusion that resolves after eating. What is the triad that points to insulinoma, and how is it treated?

cards.a: Because sulfonylureas keep working long after a single dextrose bolus wears off, hypoglycaemia can recur for hours. Admit for observation, run a dextrose infusion, give octreotide to suppress insulin release, and monitor glucose frequently.
cards.q: Why must a patient with sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia be admitted even after their glucose has recovered with dextrose?

cards.a: Admit to ICU: high fever, fast heart rate, confusion, agitation, vomiting and diarrhoea. Give a beta-blocker first to slow the heart, then propylthiouracil (PTU), then steroids, then iodine (given at least 1 hour after PTU so it does not feed hormone production). Also cool the patient and give IV fluids. Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis — do not wait for lab confirmation.
cards.q: A patient with Graves disease arrives febrile, confused, heart rate 160, after stopping methimazole. What is the diagnosis and the treatment order?

cards.a: Myxoedema coma — severe hypothyroidism with low temperature, slow heart rate, low blood pressure, confusion and slow breathing. Admit to ICU, give IV levothyroxine plus IV hydrocortisone (steroids BEFORE thyroid hormone, because thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis), rewarm slowly and support breathing.
cards.q: A patient with untreated hypothyroidism is found confused, hypothermic, bradycardic and hypotensive. What is the diagnosis and the management?

cards.a: Because giving thyroid hormone increases metabolism and cortisol clearance, which can precipitate an adrenal crisis in a patient whose adrenal glands are also underactive (common in autoimmune polyglandular disease). Steroids first protect the adrenals, then thyroid hormone can be given safely.
cards.q: In myxoedema coma, why must you give hydrocortisone before levothyroxine?

cards.a: Hypothyroidism is the most likely cause of new or worsening heart failure in an older patient with bradycardia — low thyroid hormone weakens the heart and raises cholesterol. Check thyroid function in every new heart failure case; treating the thyroid improves the heart.
cards.q: An elderly patient has new heart failure, bradycardia and high cholesterol. What endocrine cause should you check and why?

cards.a: Use methimazole (first choice in non-pregnant adults) or PTU, plus a beta-blocker for symptoms. Then choose definitive therapy: radioactive iodine or surgery. Methimazole is preferred because PTU carries a rare risk of severe liver injury; PTU is used in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm.
cards.q: A patient with Graves disease has a TSH of 0.01 and a high free T4. What are the treatment options and which antithyroid drug is preferred?

cards.a: Use PTU in the first trimester, then switch to methimazole for the second and third trimesters. Methimazole is linked to birth defects in the first trimester, while PTU carries a liver risk later. Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism in pregnancy is worse than either drug, so do not stop treatment — switch drugs.
cards.q: A pregnant patient in the first trimester has Graves disease. Which antithyroid drug should she take and why?

cards.a: Stop the antithyroid drug immediately, check a full blood count, and seek urgent haematology advice. Agranulocytosis (near-zero neutrophils) is a rare but life-threatening side effect. Tell every patient starting these drugs: fever or sore throat means stop the drug and get a blood count the same day.
cards.q: A patient on methimazole develops a fever and a sore throat. What must you do immediately and why?

cards.a: Radioactive iodine. Pregnancy is an absolute contraindication, and RAI can worsen Graves eye disease, so do not use it in a patient with active eye disease. Surgery is the alternative when RAI cannot be used.
cards.q: A pregnant patient with Graves disease asks about radioactive iodine treatment. What do you advise and why?

cards.a: Advise smoking cessation and avoid radioactive iodine, which can worsen the eye disease. Refer to ophthalmology and endocrinology. Eye disease is driven by the same antibodies, and smoking makes it worse and harder to treat.
cards.q: A patient with Graves disease has bulging eyes and double vision. What should you advise and which treatment should you avoid?

cards.a: Check TSH first. If TSH is low, do a radioactive iodine scan — a hot nodule is rarely cancer. If TSH is normal or high, get an ultrasound and consider fine-needle aspiration (FNA) based on size and suspicious features. Most thyroid nodules are benign, but the workup finds the cancers.
cards.q: A patient has a thyroid nodule on examination. What is the first test and how do you decide on biopsy?

cards.a: Surgery (usually total thyroidectomy), often followed by radioactive iodine to destroy remaining thyroid tissue, then levothyroxine to suppress TSH. Papillary thyroid cancer has an excellent prognosis, but lymph nodes in the neck must be checked at surgery.
cards.q: A fine-needle aspiration shows papillary thyroid cancer. What is the treatment and the outlook?

cards.a: Medullary thyroid cancer — it comes from calcitonin-producing C cells and is often part of MEN 2. Check calcitonin and RET genetics, and screen for phaeochromocytoma BEFORE thyroid surgery, because an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma can cause a hypertensive crisis during the operation.
cards.q: A patient has medullary thyroid cancer. What must you check before thyroid surgery and why?

cards.a: Amiodarone contains a large amount of iodine. Type 1 is iodine-driven overproduction in a gland with existing disease — stop amiodarone if possible. Type 2 is destructive thyroiditis from the drug itself — treat with steroids. Distinguishing them matters because the treatments are different.
cards.q: A patient on amiodarone develops hyperthyroidism. What are the two types and how does treatment differ?

cards.a: Treat when TSH is above 10 mIU/L, or when TSH is 5 to 10 with symptoms, positive thyroid antibodies, or goitre. Mild subclinical hypothyroidism without symptoms can be monitored instead — treating everyone with a borderline TSH does not help and causes harm.
cards.q: A patient has a TSH of 8 with a normal free T4 and no symptoms. Should you start levothyroxine?

cards.a: Take it on an empty stomach with water, 30 to 60 minutes before food, and separate it from iron, calcium and antacids by at least 4 hours. These bind levothyroxine in the gut and stop it being absorbed — a common reason for a dose that seems not to work.
cards.q: A patient on levothyroxine has a persistently high TSH despite a correct dose. What should you ask about how they take it?

cards.a: Increase the levothyroxine dose by about 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Pregnancy raises thyroid hormone demand, and untreated hypothyroidism risks miscarriage and impaired fetal brain development. Check TSH every 4 weeks during pregnancy.
cards.q: A woman on levothyroxine becomes pregnant. What should you do with her dose and why?

cards.a: Do not treat the low T3 — sick euthyroid syndrome is an adaptation to severe illness, and thyroid tests normalise as the patient recovers. Giving thyroid hormone in acute illness does not help and can cause harm. Recheck thyroid function after recovery.
cards.q: A patient in intensive care with sepsis has a low T3 and a slightly low TSH. Should you start levothyroxine?

cards.a: Subacute (painful) thyroiditis — a tender, painful thyroid after a viral illness with raised inflammatory markers. Treat with NSAIDs, or steroids if severe. The thyroid releases stored hormone first (hyperthyroid phase), then recovers — do not give antithyroid drugs, because the gland is not overproducing hormone.
cards.q: A patient has a painful, tender thyroid two weeks after a viral illness, with palpitations and a low TSH. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

cards.a: Give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately, plus large volumes of IV isotonic fluids, and correct low glucose. Do NOT wait for a cortisol level — adrenal crisis kills quickly, and the treatment is safe even if the diagnosis is wrong. Then investigate the cause and give maintenance steroids.
cards.q: A patient with known Addison's disease arrives vomiting, hypotensive and confused after a bout of gastroenteritis. What is the diagnosis and the first treatment?

cards.a: Never — in a suspected adrenal crisis, give hydrocortisone first and draw blood for cortisol at the same time, but do not wait for the result. Delay kills. The cortisol result is still useful, but treatment comes first.
cards.q: A patient looks like they are in adrenal crisis. Should you wait for the cortisol result before giving steroids?

cards.a: Double or triple the usual hydrocortisone dose during illness, fever or surgery, and switch to injectable hydrocortisone if vomiting. This is the sick-day rule. Teach patients to carry an emergency hydrocortisone injection and a steroid card, because an ordinary illness can become a crisis.
cards.q: A patient with adrenal insufficiency has influenza with a fever of 39 C. What should they do with their steroid dose?

cards.a: Add fludrocortisone, a mineralocorticoid. Primary adrenal failure (Addison's) loses aldosterone as well as cortisol, causing low sodium and high potassium. Secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary cause) keeps aldosterone, because aldosterone is controlled by renin, not ACTH — so no fludrocortisone is needed there.
cards.q: A patient with Addison's disease is on hydrocortisone but still has low sodium and high potassium. What drug should you add, and why is it not needed in secondary adrenal insufficiency?

cards.a: Use three screening tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. Two abnormal results confirm Cushing syndrome. A single test can be falsely positive, so confirmation needs more than one abnormal result.
cards.q: A patient has central obesity, purple striae and new diabetes. What tests screen for Cushing syndrome?

cards.a: If cortisol does NOT suppress after dexamethasone, Cushing syndrome is present — the gland is making cortisol autonomously and ignoring feedback. Normal suppression rules Cushing out. This test is a screening step, not a test of where the excess comes from.
cards.q: How do you interpret the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test for Cushing syndrome?

cards.a: Check ACTH: high ACTH means an ACTH-driven cause (pituitary Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH from a tumour); low ACTH means an adrenal cause. Then use high-dose dexamethasone suppression and inferior petrosal sinus sampling to distinguish pituitary from ectopic ACTH — this decides whether the pituitary or the chest is the target.
cards.q: A patient is confirmed to have Cushing syndrome. How do you find out where the excess cortisol is coming from?

cards.a: Surgery to remove the source — transsphenoidal pituitary surgery for Cushing disease, adrenalectomy for an adrenal tumour. Medical treatment (ketoconazole or metyrapone) is a bridge while waiting for surgery or when surgery is not possible — it controls cortisol but does not cure the tumour.
cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for Cushing syndrome, and what role do drugs like ketoconazole play?

cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) — it causes resistant hypertension with low potassium. Screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, confirm with a suppression test, then image the adrenals. A single adenoma is cured by adrenalectomy; bilateral hyperplasia is treated with spironolactone.
cards.q: A patient has blood pressure uncontrolled on three drugs and a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L. What diagnosis should you suspect and how is it confirmed?

cards.a: Start spironolactone. It blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor, treating both the blood pressure and the potassium loss. In resistant hypertension with low potassium, an aldosterone antagonist is often the drug that finally controls the pressure.
cards.q: A patient has resistant hypertension and low potassium and is suspected of having primary hyperaldosteronism. Which drug treats both problems?

cards.a: Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days before surgery, plus salt and fluid loading to expand the blood volume. Beta-blockers are added only AFTER alpha-blockade is established. Operating without this preparation risks a hypertensive crisis when the tumour is handled.
cards.q: A patient with phaeochromocytoma needs surgery to remove the tumour. How do you prepare them, and in what order?

cards.a: Give IV phentolamine (an alpha-blocker) or sodium nitroprusside to lower the blood pressure. Do NOT give a beta-blocker alone — it leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed and can make the crisis worse. Admit to ICU and arrange surgery once stable.
cards.q: A patient with phaeochromocytoma develops a hypertensive crisis with a BP of 240/140. What drug do you give and what must you avoid?

cards.a: Metoclopramide and glucagon can trigger catecholamine release from the tumour. Avoid them in suspected or known phaeochromocytoma, and use alternative antiemetics. Any drug that stimulates the tumour can precipitate a crisis.
cards.q: Which drugs can trigger a phaeochromocytoma crisis and must be avoided?

cards.a: Screen every adrenal incidentaloma: check for excess cortisol (dexamethasone suppression test), plasma metanephrines for phaeochromocytoma, and aldosterone and renin if the patient has hypertension or low potassium. Never biopsy an adrenal mass before excluding phaeochromocytoma — a needle can trigger a crisis.
cards.q: A CT done for another reason finds a 3 cm adrenal mass. What hormonal workup is needed before deciding what to do?
