cards.q: A patient has urethritis, conjunctivitis and arthritis together. What is this triad called, and what infection should you screen for?
cards.a: Reiter's syndrome, the classic triad of reactive arthritis. Screen for sexually transmitted infections, especially chlamydia, and for gut infections such as Salmonella, Shigella and Campylobacter. Treat the infection if it is still present, and manage the arthritis with NSAIDs.

cards.q: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops painful, swollen knees. What is the diagnosis, and what treatment caution applies?
cards.a: Enteropathic arthritis, the joint inflammation that accompanies inflammatory bowel disease. Treating the bowel disease often improves the joints. Use NSAIDs cautiously, because they can flare the bowel disease, and prefer a monoclonal TNF inhibitor, which treats both. Steroids for the joints alone are not the answer.

cards.q: A patient with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has a minor fall and now has severe, localised back pain. What must you do?
cards.a: Get a CT scan of the spine urgently. A fused, rigid spine fractures easily even with minor trauma, and the fracture is often missed on plain X-ray. A missed spinal fracture can cause cord injury and paralysis. Do not dismiss new back pain after trauma in ankylosing spondylitis as just a flare.

cards.q: A 30-year-old has back pain that is worse in the morning and at night, improves with exercise, and gets better with NSAIDs. What type of back pain is this, and what does it suggest?
cards.a: Inflammatory back pain, which suggests a spondyloarthritis such as ankylosing spondylitis. Mechanical back pain is worse with movement and better with rest, while inflammatory back pain is worse with rest and better with movement, with morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes. This pattern in a young person should prompt testing for HLA-B27 and imaging of the sacroiliac joints.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis asks what treatment works best before considering surgery. What do you recommend first?
cards.a: Weight loss if overweight, regular low-impact exercise such as walking or swimming, and physiotherapy to strengthen the quadriceps. These reduce pain and improve function as well as any drug, and they slow progression. Add topical NSAIDs for pain relief. Drugs alone without exercise and weight loss give a much poorer result.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis needs pain relief but has a history of stomach ulcer and kidney disease. What is the safest drug option?
cards.a: A topical NSAID, such as diclofenac gel, applied to the knee. It relieves pain with very little absorption into the bloodstream, so it avoids the stomach, kidney and heart risks of oral NSAIDs. Acetaminophen is another option, though it is less effective. Avoid oral NSAIDs in this patient unless there is no alternative, and then only with a proton pump inhibitor.

cards.q: A patient with knee osteoarthritis has a hot, swollen knee during a flare. What injection can help, and what should you avoid injecting?
cards.a: An intra-articular corticosteroid injection, which reduces the inflammation and pain for weeks. It is useful for flares, but should not be given repeatedly in the same joint many times a year, and must not be given if infection is suspected. Hyaluronic acid injections are not routinely recommended, as the evidence for benefit is weak.

cards.q: A patient with severe hip osteoarthritis has pain that limits walking and sleep despite weight loss, exercise, physiotherapy and painkillers. What is the next best step?
cards.a: Refer for total hip replacement. Joint replacement is the definitive treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis when pain and loss of function persist despite conservative treatment, and it reliably relieves pain and restores mobility. Do not keep adding painkillers indefinitely when the joint is worn out; the operation is the treatment.

cards.q: An elderly patient with osteoarthritis and chronic kidney disease needs pain relief. What should you avoid and what can you use instead?
cards.a: Avoid oral NSAIDs, because they reduce kidney blood flow, raise blood pressure, cause fluid retention and worsen kidney disease. Use topical NSAIDs, acetaminophen within safe daily limits, physiotherapy and weight loss instead. If pain remains severe, consider a referral for joint replacement rather than accepting the risks of long-term oral NSAIDs.

cards.q: A patient with osteoarthritis of the hands has bony lumps on the finger joints and pain when gripping. What are the lumps, and what is the treatment?
cards.a: Heberden's nodes at the DIP joints and Bouchard's nodes at the PIP joints, which are bony swellings from osteoarthritis. Treat with topical NSAIDs, hand exercises, splinting and avoiding heavy gripping. Do not give DMARDs or biologics, which are for inflammatory arthritis and do not help osteoarthritis.

cards.q: A patient with widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep and normal blood tests is diagnosed with fibromyalgia. What is the most effective treatment?
cards.a: Graded exercise, good sleep habits and cognitive behavioural therapy, with a drug such as duloxetine, pregabalin or low-dose amitriptyline if needed. Exercise is the single most effective treatment, even though it feels counterintuitive when in pain. Explain that fibromyalgia is a problem of pain processing, not joint damage, so the joints are not being destroyed.

cards.q: A patient with fibromyalgia asks for opioids or steroids for their pain. What do you advise?
cards.a: Do not use opioids or steroids for fibromyalgia. Opioids make pain worse over time through opioid-induced hyperalgesia and cause dependence, and steroids do not help because there is no inflammation to suppress. The effective treatments are exercise, sleep, psychological support and drugs such as duloxetine or pregabalin. Prescribing opioids for fibromyalgia is a common error.

cards.q: A patient with widespread pain and fatigue is found to have a very high TSH and low free T4. What is the relevance to their pain?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism can mimic fibromyalgia, causing widespread muscle pain, fatigue, stiffness and poor sleep. Always check thyroid function before diagnosing fibromyalgia, because treating the thyroid can resolve the symptoms. Other mimics to exclude are inflammatory arthritis, vitamin D deficiency and depression.

cards.q: A patient with fibromyalgia also has depression. How does treating the mood affect the pain?
cards.a: Treating the depression often improves the pain, because fibromyalgia, depression and poor sleep amplify each other through shared pathways in the brain. Drugs such as duloxetine and amitriptyline help both mood and pain. Do not treat the pain and the mood as separate problems; addressing both together gives a much better result.

cards.q: A patient has a hot, swollen knee with fever. What is the first investigation, and should you wait for the result before giving antibiotics?
cards.a: Aspirate the joint immediately and send the fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals. If the patient is unwell or the fluid looks infected, start antibiotics after the aspiration without waiting for the culture result, and get an orthopaedic opinion urgently. Delaying treatment for septic arthritis destroys the cartilage within days.

cards.q: A patient with septic arthritis of the knee is started on intravenous antibiotics. What else is essential for treatment?
cards.a: Drainage of the joint, usually by surgical washout, repeated aspiration, or arthroscopy. Antibiotics alone cannot clear pus from a closed joint space, and the infected fluid destroys cartilage quickly. Continue intravenous antibiotics for weeks, guided by the culture result and an infectious diseases opinion.

cards.q: A young sexually active patient has migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of the wrist, and small pustules on the skin. What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
cards.a: Disseminated gonococcal infection causing gonococcal arthritis. Treat with ceftriaxone, and screen for other sexually transmitted infections including chlamydia and HIV, and treat sexual partners. The joint fluid culture is often negative, so the diagnosis is clinical. Do not dismiss it as a viral arthritis.

cards.q: A patient with a knee replacement develops pain, swelling and fever 6 months after surgery. What is the concern and the management?
cards.a: Prosthetic joint infection, which is a serious complication of joint replacement. Refer urgently to orthopaedics and infectious diseases. Treatment usually requires surgery, often removal of the prosthesis and a staged revision, plus prolonged antibiotics. Do not just give oral antibiotics and hope, because bacteria form a biofilm on the metal that antibiotics cannot clear.

cards.q: A patient has a hot, swollen joint with a very high white cell count in the fluid, but the Gram stain and culture are negative. What should you do?
cards.a: Still treat as septic arthritis if the clinical suspicion is high. Cultures can be negative, especially if antibiotics were given before the aspiration, and gonococcal and some other infections are hard to grow. Also consider that gout and infection can coexist in the same joint, so finding crystals does not exclude infection. When in doubt, treat for infection.

cards.q: A patient about to start a biologic drug has never had the shingles vaccine. What should you do, and why does the timing matter?
cards.a: Give the recombinant shingles vaccine before starting the biologic if possible, and avoid live vaccines once immunosuppression has started. Biologics and JAK inhibitors raise the risk of shingles, and live vaccines are unsafe on immunosuppression because the weakened virus can cause disease. Inactivated vaccines should be given before or during treatment, but live vaccines must be given at least 4 weeks before starting.

cards.q: A patient on methotrexate is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection. What is the problem with this combination?
cards.a: Both drugs suppress the bone marrow, and together they can cause severe pancytopenia, a dangerous drop in all blood cells. Avoid the combination: choose a different antibiotic for the infection, or hold the methotrexate. This is a classic drug interaction that is easy to miss because both drugs are common.

cards.q: A patient on azathioprine for lupus is started on allopurinol for gout. What is the danger, and what must you do?
cards.a: Allopurinol blocks the breakdown of azathioprine, so azathioprine levels rise sharply and cause severe bone marrow suppression. Either avoid the combination or reduce the azathioprine dose to about a quarter and monitor blood counts very closely. This interaction is a common cause of life-threatening pancytopenia.

cards.q: A patient on hydroxychloroquine is started on another drug that prolongs the QT interval. What should you check?
cards.a: Check an ECG for QT prolongation, because hydroxychloroquine can prolong the QT interval and the combination increases the risk of a dangerous arrhythmia. Check potassium and magnesium too, since low levels worsen the risk. Review the drug list for other QT-prolonging drugs and stop or replace them where possible.

cards.q: A patient with RA takes daily prednisone and an NSAID together. What extra drug should you prescribe, and why?
cards.a: A proton pump inhibitor, because steroids plus NSAIDs together greatly increase the risk of stomach ulcer and gastrointestinal bleeding. Either drug alone raises the risk, but the combination is much worse. Do not wait for stomach pain to appear; the first sign of a bleed can be a life-threatening haemorrhage.

cards.q: A patient will be on prednisone 10 mg daily for many months for a rheumatic disease. What bone and infection precautions are needed?
cards.a: Give calcium and vitamin D, and a bisphosphonate to prevent steroid-induced osteoporosis, since bone loss is fastest in the first months of steroids. Monitor blood pressure and blood sugar, and consider Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole if the dose is high or combined with another immunosuppressant. Long-term steroids need a prevention plan, not just a prescription.
